_note: Checklist drafted by Claude from the real CMS policy text (L34220, L36575, L36861) on 2026-10-24. A billing lead or clinician should review it. Only the main coverage path of each policy is modeled (e.g. knee revisions and fractures are not).

groups.description: Reason for the MRI (at least one)

criteria.text: A red flag is documented from the history and physical exam: major trauma, minor trauma in a potentially osteoporotic patient, history of cancer, fever, chills, unexplained weight loss, recent bacterial infection, IV drug abuse, immune suppression, pain that worsens when supine or at night, saddle anesthesia, recent onset of bladder dysfunction, clinically significant or progressive neurologic deficit or motor weakness in the lower extremity, unexpected laxity of the anal sphincter, perianal or perineal sensory loss, or other nerve root compromise.
With no red flag: low back symptoms have lasted more than one month and the patient has not responded to a reasonable trial of conservative management lasting at least four weeks.
History and physical examination findings are documented, such as muscle strength, reflexes, sensation, or straight leg raise.
The MRI result will be used for medical decision-making: surgery or other aggressive treatment (for example an injection) is being considered, or a serious condition must be ruled out.

Imaging (X-ray, or MRI/CT when X-ray is not adequate) shows advanced joint disease: subchondral cysts, subchondral sclerosis, periarticular osteophytes, joint subluxation, joint space narrowing, or avascular necrosis.
Pain or functional disability from injury due to trauma or arthritis of the knee joint.

Unsuccessful conservative therapy is clearly documented: anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics, flexibility and strengthening exercises, supervised physical therapy, assistive device use, weight reduction, or therapeutic knee injections.

The record explains why conservative therapy would be ineffective or inappropriate, for example bone-on-bone articulation, severe deformity, or significant disabling interference with activities of daily living.
No active infection is present (knee joint, systemic bacteremia, urinary tract, dental, or skin infection or open wound at the surgical site) and no rapidly progressive neurological disease.
Clinical signs and symptoms indicative of obstructive sleep apnea are documented, such as loud snoring, witnessed apneas or gasping during sleep, or excessive daytime sleepiness.

Symptoms of narcolepsy severe enough to interfere with the patient's well-being and health: inappropriate sleep episodes or attacks (for example while driving or eating), amnesiac episodes, or continuous disabling drowsiness.
A suspected parasomnia (for example REM sleep behavior disorder, sleepwalking, or sleep terrors) that is injurious or not clearly diagnosed by clinical evaluation.
The study is not being done only for chronic insomnia, insomnia related to depression, circadian rhythm disorders, or restless legs or periodic limb movements unrelated to a covered condition.
